fields.title: Versta: The Contract Includes What Doesn't Exist in the Product
fields.summary: The deal is signed, and the integration is promised for launch in nine weeks. Decide what to do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do this week and what will you promise the client?
fields.brief/role: You are the integration product manager at Versta.
fields.brief/company: Versta is a fictional company of 250 people that sells an HR record system to mid-sized employers.
fields.brief/context: On Friday, a deal worth 18 million rubles per year was closed. This morning, implementation reported that the signed order contains a line: 'two-way synchronization with the Delta payroll system, available at launch'. Launch is in nine weeks. No such integration is planned or in development. The sales manager points to a chat from three months ago where an engineer wrote: 'if we build Delta, it will probably be in the second half of the year'.
fields.brief/objective: Fulfill the commitment so that the client gets a working process, without the team missing a mandatory deadline on another project.
fields.brief/constraints: Nine weeks until launch. Five team members are busy with a regulatory requirement that has an unmovable deadline.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: First find out what was promised, then decide how to deliver
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A word in a contract and the client's actual problem are different things, and the gap between them is usually wider than it seems: a single call can turn an eight-week job into a three-week one. You need to solve the problem and document it with acceptance criteria, otherwise the same dispute will return at the next renewal. Separately, you must fix the process that allowed the promise to appear in the first place.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Section 3 of the order: 'Two-way synchronization of payroll data with the Delta system, available at client launch.' One of eleven lines.

The lawyer confirms: this is a contractual obligation, not marketing copy.

Chat from three months ago:
manager: 'Do we support Delta?'
engineer: 'Not today. If we build it, it will probably be in the second half of the year, it's on the long list.'
manager: 'Got it.'

There are no other records. The lawyer reviewed the contract terms, but product approval is not required during the ordering process: anyone in sales can add a line to an order.

This has already happened twice over the past year, and both times we got away with it.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
From a conversation with the head of integrations:

'Delta has an open API. One-way export of employee profiles is realistic: about three weeks for one engineer. It covers the case where HR data goes from us to payroll.

Two-way synchronization is a different story. They don't have change notifications, which means polling on a schedule; given their limitations, a full reconciliation for a client with 2,000 people takes about forty minutes. The hardest part is conflict resolution when a record is edited on both sides. Realistically, it's eight to ten weeks for two people, and I wouldn't give the first version of that to a client at launch.'
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The head of implementation called the client's HR director before everyone started panicking.

Reason for the request: the payroll team currently manually re-enters new employees and salary changes from the old system into Delta—about 90 records per month, with errors.

When asked what 'two-way' meant to her, she replied: 'Honestly, that was the salesperson's word. We just need hiring and salary changes to get into payroll without manual entry.'

The reverse flow of payroll data back into the HR system is described as 'nice to have someday': the payroll team owns that, and they have no plans to change their setup.

Launch for them is January 1st, the date in the official order.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
CTO: 'A chat message is not a commitment. I will not pull people off the regulatory project.'

Commercial Director: 'The deal is closed, the revenue is already in this quarter. Whatever you do, don't back out.' He hasn't been told the details yet.

The sales manager apologizes, saying he sincerely believed in the second half of the year. He hasn't done anything like this before.

Head of Implementation: 'I can handle almost anything if I know exactly what it is next week. What I can't do is find out on week seven.'

Product Lead: 'Decide for yourself. Tell me what you need from me.'
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: One-way for launch, two-way with a set date
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Build the export in three weeks, get written agreement from the client on what exactly works at launch and when the rest will be delivered, and fix the order creation process.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
A conversation with the HR director shows that 'two-way' was just the salesperson's word: she needs hiring and salary changes to get into payroll without manual entry. This is exactly a one-way export.
You define the commitment as acceptance criteria: 90 records per month go to Delta without manual entry, delay is under an hour, conflicts are logged and resolved by a human.
You sign an addendum: one-way for launch, reverse flow with a date in the next quarter, without promising 'two-way' as a term.
Implementation learns the scope in week one instead of week seven and has time to adjust the plan.
Separately, you introduce product approval for order lines mentioning integration: the two previous cases went fine, but a third one would have cost more.
Compromise: you had to explain to the Commercial Director why the addendum used a different word, which was an unpleasant conversation.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The positions of the CTO and Commercial Director contradict each other. Pass the decision to leadership and do not talk to the client until it is resolved.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
A meeting is scheduled in a week and a half because both directors have busy calendars.
At the meeting, the first question is what exactly the client needs—and it turns out no one has asked. The question is kicked back to you.
You make the same call you could have made on day one and return with the answer a week later.
You are left with six weeks instead of nine; implementation learns the scope in week three.
Compromise: the escalation level was correct—the order creation process is indeed beyond your control—but finding out the client's problem was escalated along with it, which was your job.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Remove the line and offer a discount
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Admit that the feature was promised by mistake, cross it out of the contract, and compensate with a price reduction.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The client takes this harder than expected: they do not want a discount, they want to stop manually re-entering 90 records per month.
The HR director—your internal champion—ends up looking like someone who brought her colleagues a solution with a broken promise.
Meanwhile, a one-way export that solves her problem would take three weeks and was entirely feasible.
The deal is saved, but the relationship is damaged, and this incident will be remembered at renewal.
Compromise: the commitment was settled with money instead of finding out what was behind it.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Fulfill the contract literally: pull two people onto Delta for nine weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Two people are pulled off the regulatory project, which has an unmovable deadline, and it starts falling behind.
The synchronization itself is not ready by week nine: eight to ten weeks was an estimate without conflict resolution and reconciliation for 2,000 people, and the head of integrations advised against launching the first version of this.
By week seven, it becomes clear you won't make it, and the conversation with the client happens anyway—just later and under worse circumstances.
Meanwhile, the reverse flow that you rushed to build was only needed 'someday' by the client.
Compromise: you fulfilled the contract literally without checking what was behind the phrasing, and paid for it with a second broken commitment.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Requirements were gathered from the loudest person, not from everyone who can block the project
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A stakeholder with high influence and low interest was ignored until the very end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The current way of working is not considered as the primary alternative
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A request was mistaken for a task: the phrasing lacks a verifiable 'so that'
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Scope was cut based on importance rather than user journey coherence
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: 'Done' was not defined by a verifiable condition before starting work
